title: Working-memory architecture
content_html:
Working-memory architecture

Alan Baddeley’s model (widely used in cognitive psychology) proposes that working memory isn’t a unitary space, but a system of specialized buffers coordinated by a control system. A central executive oversees attention, task switching, inhibition, and allocation of resources, but doesn’t store much information itself. Other processes form a multimodal workspace that integrates info across domains (verbal, visual, long-term memory). Together they provide a unified “scene” or “episode” from otherwise separate streams. Capacity differs across subsystems (e.g., phonological loop may hold ~2 seconds of speech; visuospatial span often 3–4 objects). Working memory is not a single box; it’s a coordinated set of specialized stores, with capacity limits around 3–4 integrated chunks of information at once.

This all matters because it explains limits in multitasking, learning, and reasoning. It is the groundwork for understanding working memory deficits in conditions like ADHD, dyslexia, or aging, and nforms design of education (e.g., cognitive load theory in instructional design).

The working-memory architecture and capacity theory is important because it explains how the mind actively holds and manipulates information in the moment - the “mental workspace” that underpins nearly all higher cognition. It explains why our minds feel overloaded: ~3–4 chunks is a natural bottleneck. This capacity limit is one of the most robust findings in cognitive psychology. Domain-specific buffers (phonological, visuospatial) reveal that verbal and visual information use different temporary stores - crucial for understanding learning and communication. Integration via the episodic buffer provides the mechanism for binding across modalities and with long-term memory - how we form “episodes” or coherent experiences.

This model is a conceptual backbone for education, clinical psychology, human factors, and AI models of cognition, because it highlights the bottlenecks and structures of thought - not just how much we can hold, but how we integrate different kinds of information. Practically, it guides how we teach, design, and support people to think and act effectively under real cognitive constraints.
